claim_verdicts.evidence: .NET 10 API docs, RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(Int32): "Creates an array of bytes with a cryptographically strong random sequence of values." / returns "An array populated with cryptographically strong random values." The docs document strength/unpredictability; they never promise two calls differ. Execution supports the practical point: two Hash("donhang-dev-password") calls gave salts XtcnrvaYtvNkcQF6keQzQQ== and 2cVeVsThtaZVCP8x2xlVoQ==. "never ... in practice" is a probability statement, not a documented guarantee.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes fills the array with a cryptographically strong random sequence of values, so each call returns an unpredictable 16-byte salt; two salts colliding is not something any real run will produce.

claim_verdicts.evidence: .NET 10 API docs, CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(ReadOnlySpan<Byte>, ReadOnlySpan<Byte>): "Determines the equality of two byte sequences in an amount of time that depends on the length of the sequences, but not their values." Remarks: "compares the contents from two buffers for equality in a way that doesn't leak timing information" and "will short-circuit and return false only if left and right have different lengths". In Verify both spans have length expected.Length, so the short-circuit case never applies.

No allowed source states PBKDF2 irreversibility. Tried: (a) Grep of refs/dotnet-docs - cryptographic-services.md covers only collision resistance ("computationally infeasible to find two distinct inputs that hash to the same value"), not preimages; (b) learn.microsoft.com Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2 (net-10.0) says only "Fills a buffer with a PBKDF2 derived key"; (c) RFC 8018 / NIST SP 800-132 are not docs roots in versions.yaml. Nearest allowed line, CA5387: "A higher iteration count can help mitigate against dictionary attacks that try to guess the ... key" - guessing, not inversion.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Nothing stored here can be turned back into the password by computation: the stored value is a derived key, and the only route back is guessing a password and hashing it again — which the 100,000 iterations are there to make slow.

issues.text: Overstated against the source. AuthController.Login returns Unauthorized() when no customer matches the email or when customer.PasswordHash is null — in both cases PasswordHasher.Verify never runs, so the hash comparison is not the only thing deciding the outcome. Section 4 gets this right ("once the customer's row is found"); section 2 does not.
issues.quote: and only that comparison decides whether the login succeeds
issues.fix: Rewrite as: "...checks a submitted password against this value through `PasswordHasher.Verify`; once the customer's row is found, that comparison is what decides whether the login succeeds."

issues.text: Two absolutes the allowed documentation does not support, and that a junior will read as 'a stolen hash column is harmless'. A hash cannot be inverted by computation, but whoever reads the column can guess candidate passwords and re-hash them — which is exactly why Iterations is 100_000 (CA5387: 'A higher iteration count can help mitigate against dictionary attacks that try to guess the generated cryptographic key'). Same overstatement in section 6: 'A hash never reveals the original password even to someone who reads it.'
issues.quote: there's no way back from a hash to the password it came from, by design
issues.fix: Condition both sentences on computation, not on secrecy: section 4 -> "nothing computes the password back from a hash; the only route back is guessing a password and hashing it again, which the 100,000 iterations make slow". Section 6 -> "A hash doesn't hand the original password to whoever reads it; recovering it means guessing, one slow hash at a time."

issues.text: Unlisted claim: "a higher count makes computing one hash slower, on purpose" is a behaviour/number statement about PBKDF2 that appears nowhere in .meta.json's claims. It happens to be true — measured with dotnet 10.0.300 on this machine, Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(SHA256, 32 bytes): 10,000 iterations 21 ms, 100,000 iterations 103 ms, 1,000,000 iterations 1054 ms — but the ledger must carry it so a later version bump re-checks it.
issues.quote: iteration count — how many times the transformation repeats; a higher count makes computing one hash slower, on purpose
issues.fix: Add a claim to .meta.json: n=8, kind "behavior", version_key "dotnet", section 3, text "PBKDF2 cost grows with the iteration count; a higher count makes one hash computation proportionally slower, which is what slows down guessing", source_hint "CA5387 (dotnet docs) + measured 10k/100k/1M iterations". Leave the lesson sentence as written.

issues.text: Fill answer set is incomplete and contains one entry that cannot go in the blank. The blank is `var salt = ____.GetBytes(SaltSize);`; "RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes" substituted there yields `RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes.GetBytes(SaltSize)`. The fully qualified spelling a learner may type, "System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator", is valid C# here and is not accepted.

The key (a) is right, but the distractor explanation for option c is factually backwards. `==` on two byte[] is a reference comparison — a single pointer check — so it is strictly faster than FixedTimeEquals, which reads every byte of both buffers. Saying FixedTimeEquals 'is not meaningfully faster than ==' invites the reader to think the two cost the same.
issues.fix: Rewrite explanation c as: "Speed is not the reason — `==` on two byte arrays only compares references, so it is the cheaper operation; `FixedTimeEquals` reads every byte on purpose, to keep the duration independent of the contents."

issues.text: Ordering is unambiguous and the key b,d,c,a matches the code, but option a ('The caller (`AuthController.Login`) receives true or false') is not a step of `PasswordHasher.Verify` — it happens after Verify returns — while the stem says 'these four steps of `PasswordHasher.Verify`'.
issues.quote: Put these four steps of `PasswordHasher.Verify` in the order they run.
issues.fix: Change the stem to: "Put these four steps of a login password check in the order they run." Keep the answer b, d, c, a.
